sources.title: Inō Tadataka (Q1240937), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): English label 'Inō Tadataka', description 'Japanese surveyor and cartographer (1745-1818)', Korean label 이노 다다타카, born 11 February 1745, died 17 May 1818, citizenship Japan. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.
Wikipedia, 'Inō Tadataka' (English article, read as orientation only). Not counted as a substantive source and not used as support for any row or card.

Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (national mapping agency), exhibition page 'The Ino Maps: the origin of modern maps, commemorating 200 years since the completion of the Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu' (2021), read in full (Japanese). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Ino Tadataka began surveying Ezo in 1800 at 55 and carried out ten surveys to 1816, producing a surveyed map from Hokkaido to Kyushu; he died in 1818, his disciples took the work on, and the Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu (the Ino maps) was completed in 1821 and submitted to the shogunate, with large (1:36,000, 214 sheets), medium (1:216,000, 8 sheets) and small (1:432,000, 3 sheets) scales; the official copy burned in the palace fire of 1873 and the Ino family copy given to the government was lost in the 1923 earthquake; the exhibition presents how the Ino maps influenced later Japanese mapping. The page prints his birth year as 1754, a typographical slip against every other source (1745).

Hoshino Yoshihisa, 'Mapping a Nation: Japan's Most Famous Cartographer, Inō Tadataka', Nippon.com, Shapers of Japanese History series (30 January 2020), read in full: a detailed narrative of his life and surveys (merchant and village headman, retirement at 49, study with Takahashi Yoshitoki, the 1800 Ezo survey, the 1803 presentation to the shogun, asthma and malaria on later trips, the 1821 completion by his students, the loss of the originals), with a candid closing paragraph on his sternness with people and the limits on his longitude accuracy.

'Inō, Tadataka', Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Charles Scribner's Sons, 2008; the entry text as reproduced by Encyclopedia.com), read in full: a scholarly entry that explains the meridian-length problem, the 1800 survey and the western surveys, and the maps' later use, and that also lists his scientific limits (traverse method rather than triangulation, a spherical earth, no allowance for refraction, parallax or nutation, longitudes fixed by measured distances) and the secrecy that limited the maps' influence. Its bibliography names Otani Ryokichi's 1917 biography as the standard life.

Japan Search (National Diet Library portal), 'Tadataka Ino' (person page with a biographical note), read: a short institutional note recording his adoption by the Ino family, his revival of its sake-brewing and rice-trading business, retirement at 50, study under Takahashi Yoshitoki in Edo, ten surveys over 18 years, and the explanation given to the shogunate that the Ezo survey mattered for northern defence while the master and pupil first wanted the distance of a degree of latitude; it also records that Mamiya Rinzo surveyed the rest of Ezo and that Takahashi Kageyasu and others completed the Ino maps.

BRUTUS magazine web article on the 'Ino Walk' (Japanese, undated; the guide quoted is a walking-trip specialist), read in full: popular, partly promotional account of the ten surveys, the shift from largely self-funded surveys to an official project from the fifth survey, the devised bearing-compass instrument, his illness in later years, and the statement that his work involved no compromise; the article itself marks the 'forty million steps' figure as legend.

National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, Tokyo, news item 'Report on Important Cultural Properties Designation Submitted' (March 2010), read: records the Council for Cultural Affairs' report designating 2,345 materials pertaining to Inō Tadataka (maps, documents and surveying instruments, Katori City) as National Treasures. A short factual notice; used only for the 2010 designation.

Katori City, Ino Tadataka Memorial Museum, object page 'Portrait of Ino Tadataka' (Japanese), read: the museum describes it as Ino Tadataka's only portrait painting and says it was probably painted by his disciple Aoki Katsujiro when his grandson presented the Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu to the shogunate after his death; file 1244 x 3352 px. The city's site policy page states that copyright in the site's text and images belongs to the city or the content provider and that reuse needs permission; the object page itself gives no licence.

National Diet Library Digital Collections, Otani Ryokichi (ed.), Inō Tadataka (Tokyo: Iwanami Shoten, 1917), item-level Public Domain Mark: the printed plate captioned 'Portrait of Ino Tadataka' near the front of the book. Opened for the portrait only; the book text was not read.

persistence.rationale: [src_ino_gsi, src_ino_jpsearch, src_ino_nippon, src_ino_brutus, src_ino_dsb | 1800-1818 | national mapping agency, library portal, journalist, popular magazine, scholarly encyclopedia] Five independent descriptions agree on a sustained programme: ten surveys from 1800 to 1816 (GSI), 17-18 years, thousands of kilometres on foot (nippon, Japan Search, Brutus); nippon adds that he suffered asthma and contracted malaria on a later trip and had to lay down his instruments during bouts of illness, and Brutus says he largely did not take part in the last two surveys, so the persistence is documented and also bounded by age and illness. The project was also carried by a team and by state funding (nippon credits Takahashi, his son and the government), so the row scores his own sustained effort, not the whole enterprise. 'Forty million steps' is legend and is not used.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_ino_nippon, src_ino_dsb, src_ino_jpsearch | 1794-1800 | journalist, scholarly encyclopedia, library portal] At 49 he handed the business to his son and moved to Edo, where he threw himself into astronomy and became a pupil of Takahashi Yoshitoki (nippon, Japan Search); he then set himself the problem of the size of the earth, and the Dictionary of Scientific Biography says he volunteered to undertake a geodetic survey, with Takahashi negotiating permission in 1800. The sequence (retire, retrain, propose and begin a survey) is documented by three independent writers; the motive attributed to him is the scholars' account of the meridian problem, not a quotation.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_ino_nippon, src_ino_jpsearch, src_ino_dsb, src_ino_brutus | 1800-1805 | journalist, library portal, scholarly encyclopedia, popular magazine] Three separate facts: he supplemented the modest stipend with personal funds, and until the fourth survey most of the money was his own (nippon, Brutus); the survey was put to the shogunate as important for northern defence, which Japan Search and the Dictionary of Scientific Biography both give as the route to permission, while the astronomers' own aim was the length of a degree; and Brutus says he devised the bearing compass fixed to a staff that he used most (a popular source). The defence framing is reported as the way the project was sanctioned, and is not scored as politics.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_ino_dsb, src_ino_nippon, src_ino_brutus | 1800-1816 | scholarly encyclopedia, journalist, popular magazine] The scholarly entry reports measurement by steps and bearings by day and a star's altitude at night, over 2,000 latitude determinations on the western survey, giving a meridian figure within a few tenths of a second of the figure in Lalande; nippon says latitude was determined to impressive accuracy from meridian altitudes. Brutus says he entered unsurveyable difficult sections honestly on the map and even asked to resurvey them, but that rests on 'it is said' wording and is treated only as colour. Limit: the same scholarly entry says he ignored refraction, parallax and nutation, treated the earth as a sphere and fixed longitude by distance, so the row is carefulness in field measurement, not theoretical rigour.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_ino_nippon, src_ino_dsb, src_ino_brutus | 1795-1800 | journalist, scholarly encyclopedia, popular magazine] His formal scientific study began only at fifty (DSB); nippon says that under Takahashi he mastered fixing his position by celestial bodies, and Brutus (popular) says he improved so much that even his master was surprised and was recommended for the Ezo survey within five years. The documented fact is a second-career apprenticeship that reached working competence; the surprise of the teacher is a popular-magazine statement, so the row stays low in confidence.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_ino_nippon, src_ino_brutus | 1800-1816 | journalist, popular magazine] He led a small party in 1800 whose maps impressed the shogunal leaders; after the 1803 presentation the survey became an official project, his team grew to include calendar-office experts, and he was made a retainer (nippon, Brutus). Nippon also calls him a shrewd leader who was stern and inflexible with people, even to turning out pupils for offences; that is a documented cost to the working relationships, so the impact is dual-edged. Only two writers describe the team and the sternness is from one, hence the low confidence.

portrait.source: Printed plate captioned 'Portrait of Ino Tadataka' in Otani Ryokichi (ed.), Ino Tadataka (Tokyo: Iwanami Shoten, 1917), as digitised by the National Diet Library (NDL Digital Collections item 956854, page image R0000004). It reproduces the painted portrait of about 1821 kept by the Ino Tadataka Memorial Museum in Katori, which the museum says is his only portrait and was probably painted by his disciple Aoki Katsujiro after his death. The file is the plate cropped from the library's 4064 x 2848 pixel scan of the book spread (756 x 988 pixels), black-and-white halftone, with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain (National Diet Library item-level Public Domain Mark; a 1917 Japanese publication reproducing a painting of about 1821)
portrait.attribution: Painting probably by Aoki Katsujiro (c. 1821, attributed by the Ino Tadataka Memorial Museum, Katori); plate in Otani Ryokichi (ed.), Ino Tadataka, Iwanami Shoten, 1917; digitised by the National Diet Library, Japan (https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/956854)
portrait.creator: Aoki Katsujiro (attributed)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / RESOLVED WITH THE SAME PAINTING FROM A BETTER HOLDER. The lead (Commons 'Ino Tadataka.jpg', tagged public domain by age, source the Katori City Ino Tadataka Memorial Museum object page) was checked at the holder: the Katori object page (opened) says it is his only portrait painting, probably painted by his disciple Aoki Katsujiro after his death when his grandson presented the Dai Nihon Enkai Yochi Zenzu to the shogunate (so about 1821, posthumous, not 'dated 1821 lifetime' as the lead noted); it carries no licence, and the city's site policy page (opened) says copyright in the site's images belongs to the city or the content provider and reuse needs permission. A painting of about 1821 is public domain by age, but the holder's blanket claim over the image file weakens that route as 'strong', so I did not use the Katori file. Instead I found the same painting reproduced as a printed plate captioned 'Portrait of Ino Tadataka' in Otani Ryokichi (ed.), Ino Tadataka (Iwanami Shoten, 1917), a National Diet Library Digital Collections item (pid 956854, IIIF canvas R0000004) whose IIIF manifest metadata gives 'Access Restrictions: PDM' (Public Domain Mark) at item level. A 1917 Japanese publication is public domain in Japan and in the US (published before 1931), so the URAA question does not arise. Holder verification: NDL manifest read (title, creator, publisher, 1917, PDM); the book text was not read. I compared the plate with the Commons colour image and it is the same composition. The crop (756 x 988 px from a 4064 x 2848 spread scan; the plate itself is small, no upscaling) is a black-and-white halftone, so it looks worse than the colour Commons file, a deliberate choice of the legally clearer route. Kind historical_depiction (a posthumous painting, not a sitting). ZERO POLITICS: primary identity surveyor, astronomer and cartographer; the shogunal retainer status and the defence rationale are context, not scored. VOCABULARY: occupations scientist and astronomer, fields natural_science and exploration, tags field_researcher and career_changer, archetype scientific_explorer, impact domains scientific and historical, all existing with EN and KO labels. KO NAME: Wikidata Korean label 이노 다다타카 (short, standard). ATTRIBUTION: attribution_screen_result attributable CONFIRMED: dated, documented surveys and a surviving body of maps, diaries and instruments (2,345 National Treasure items); the profile rests on modern institutional and scholarly accounts of dated surveys, and nothing is scored from legend. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Geospatial Information Authority of Japan exhibition page (src_ino_gsi). READ (8 incl. Wikidata and Wikipedia; 6 substantive): (1) GSI exhibition page, full; (2) nippon.com Shapers of Japanese History, full; (3) Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry via Encyclopedia.com, full; (4) Japan Search (NDL) person page, read; (5) BRUTUS Ino Walk article, full (popular, partly promotional); (6) NRICP news item on the 2010 National Treasure designation (short). Plus the Katori museum portrait page and the NDL book plate for the portrait only. PERSPECTIVES: national mapping agency, national library portal, a scholarly biographical dictionary, an English-language journalist on a foundation-run site, a popular magazine, a heritage-designation notice. COUNTER-VOICES AND LIMITS: the Dictionary of Scientific Biography says he was an energetic observer who did not excel at devising new methods or theories, used the traverse rather than triangulation, treated the earth as a sphere, ignored refraction, parallax and nutation, and fixed longitude by measured distances so Hokkaido carries a systematic error; nippon says longitude was his weak point, that he was stern and inflexible with people and that the official maps were never published and the originals were lost; both stress state backing and the help of the Takahashi family. NOT OPENED: M. William Steele, 'The Man who Walked 40 Million Steps' (Asian Cultural Studies 45, 2019; the ICU repository returned HTTP 503 for maintenance), Otani Ryokichi's 1917 biography text, Ino's own diaries and treatises (self-report, not accessed), Wikipedia details (3,736 days, 34,913 km, 19 members) which were not corroborated in a counted source and are not used. EXCLUSIONS: his family quarrels and private life (nippon mentions disowning his children) are not used; the 'forty million steps' figure is legend; discrepancies noted: GSI prints 1754 for his birth, nippon and Brutus say 17 years of surveying while Japan Search says 18 years, and Japan Search puts his retirement at 50 where nippon says 49. SPARSE PROFILE: 6 rows, scores 62-76, confidence 0.48-0.64; no row above 0.64 because there is no adversarial behavioural biographer and the two most detailed sources are a popular article and a one-volume scholarly entry. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk rows reviewed: persistence (highest score; kept at 76/0.64 because five independent institutional and press descriptions agree on the 17-year programme and the illness and the age limits are already stated in the rationale), proactive_agency (kept: three independent writers document retire, retrain and propose, and the confidence is already the strong_inference band), leadership_drive (kept at 62/0.48: only two writers and already low-confidence inference). No row lowered.
